title: Customer Credit Risk
answer: Customer credit risk is the chance that a buyer will not pay what they owe on the terms agreed, and it sits at the centre of receivables work. In practice it covers the whole book of customers rather than single invoices, from setting a credit limit before the first order to deciding what to do when an account goes past due. It also reaches into payables, because a company's own payment behaviour shapes how its suppliers and lenders judge it. The work is usually split between a credit team, collections, and finance, with the same data feeding all three.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Customer credit risk is the chance that a buyer will not pay what they owe on the terms agreed, and it sits at the centre of receivables work. In practice it covers the whole book of customers rather than single invoices, from setting a credit limit before the first order to deciding what to do when an account goes past due. It also reaches into payables, because a company's own payment behaviour shapes how its suppliers and lenders judge it. The work is usually split between a credit team, collections, and finance, with the same data feeding all three.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the transaction record: invoices, due dates, payment history, order volumes, and any external reports a business chooses to buy. That data usually lives in an ERP or accounting system, with a separate credit or collections tool layered on top, and spreadsheets still fill the gaps in many finance teams. Models range from simple rule sets and scorecards to machine learning classifiers that rank accounts by likelihood of late or missed payment. The output has to land back in the systems people already use, which is why integration work often matters more than the modelling itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical build starts by defining what counts as a bad outcome, such as payment more than a set number of days late or a write-off, then labelling historical accounts against that definition. Features are drawn from payment behaviour, order patterns, and any permitted external data, and the model is trained and tested on periods held back from the training set. Because default is rare, teams often adjust for class imbalance and check that the model still works across customer segments and seasons. The result is reviewed by credit staff rather than applied blindly, and thresholds are tuned to the business's appetite for risk and for chasing customers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Credit decisions affect real people and real firms, so they attract consumer and commercial credit rules, data protection duties, and internal audit scrutiny. A model that denies credit or cuts a limit needs a documented reason, a route for the customer to ask questions, and evidence that it does not discriminate on protected grounds. Provenance matters too: teams should be able to say which data trained the model, how old it is, and who approved each version.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more use of cash flow and bank data, where the customer consents to share it, alongside the traditional credit bureau file. Larger finance teams are moving from periodic scorecards to continuous monitoring that flags a deteriorating account between reporting cycles. Explainability and audit trails will keep growing in importance as regulators and auditors ask harder questions about automated decisions. The practical direction is fewer standalone credit models and more credit signals embedded in the everyday tools that raise an invoice, chase a payment, and close the books.
